l8-pool-tendencies: Every stake's player pool has specific shared tendencies. For example, micro-stakes players usually call too much and aren't aggressive enough; mid-stakes players may 3-Bet too much but give up too fast postflop.

The core of exploitation: find the direction where opponents/the pool deviate from GTO, then adjust in the opposite direction. Opponent calls too much? Increase value bets, reduce bluffs. Opponent folds too much? Increase bluff frequency.

Micro-stakes (NL2-NL10):
• Call too much, rarely fold
• Response: pure value betting, almost no bluffs

Low-stakes (NL25-NL50):
• Preflop becoming reasonable but weak postflop
• Response: more C-Bets, more double barrels

Mid-stakes (NL100-NL200):
• Strategy close to GTO but still has leaks
• Response: precise node locking + small exploitation
Don't use high-stakes strategies against micro-stakes. At micro-stakes, pure value betting and abandoning bluffs may make more than GTO.

Exploitation adjustment-size formula:
Safe deviation = observable deviation × (1 - opponent adjustment probability)

Example: opponent river fold rate 70% (equilibrium ~50%)
Observable deviation = +20%
Assume opponent adjustment probability = 30% (low-stakes players adjust slowly)
Safe deviation = 20% × (1-0.3) = 14%

This means you can raise your bluff frequency by about 14 percentage points,
but be ready to return to baseline (if the opponent starts adjusting)

Exploitation magnitude isn't "bigger is better" — it's capped by "not being counter-exploited"

Theory reference: the full framework of player typology and exploitation adjustments is in Theory Academy T7 Chapter 4 "Exploitative Adjustment Mapping". HUD metric combination interpretation is in T7 Chapters 1-2. The GTO-exploitation unified framework is in T9 Chapter 4.

Counter-intuitive: the bigger your exploitation, the easier you get counter-exploited. When you deviate heavily from the GTO baseline to exploit an opponent, your own strategy develops obvious leaks that experienced opponents can exploit in turn. That's why exploitative adjustments should be "minimum necessary deviations" — capturing profit while keeping room to pivot.
l8-population-analysis: From Individual Analysis to Population Analysis

When you have no data on a specific opponent, use the "average tendencies" of that stake's players as the default assumption. That's Population Analysis — analyzing the statistical tendencies of a specific player pool.

Key statistical metrics:
• Pool average VPIP/PFR: determines the pool's looseness/tightness
• Fold to C-Bet %: determines your C-Bet frequency
• Fold to 3-Bet %: determines your 3-Bet bluff frequency
• WTSD% (Went to Showdown): judges multi-street bluff effectiveness

If the pool's average Fold to C-Bet = 65% (far above GTO's 45%):
→ You should C-Bet more frequently (even 100% on dry boards)

If the pool's average Fold to 3-Bet = 70%:
→ You can significantly widen your 3-Bet bluff range

If the pool's average WTSD = 28% (high):
→ Reduce multi-street bluffs, increase value bets
Use population data as a "default assumption", then gradually shift to individualized exploitation as you learn a specific opponent.
l8-exploitative-adjustments: GTO vs Exploitative: When to Use Which?
GTO is an "unexploitable" defensive strategy; Exploitative is an "maximize opponent weakness" offensive strategy. In practice, combine both.

Use GTO when: opponent unknown, opponent very strong, multiway pots.
Use exploitation when: opponent has clear leaks, you have enough data, heads-up spots.

vs a Nit (ultra-tight):
• Steal blinds relentlessly
• Fold immediately when he raises
• Don't bluff him

vs a Calling Station:
• Pure value betting, never bluff
• Slightly larger bet sizing
• Respect his raises

vs a Maniac:
• Patiently wait for strong hands
• Call down with medium strength
• Don't bluff him
• Control pot size

Exploitative strategies are inherently "unbalanced":
• If the opponent notices and adjusts, you can lose
• Don't over-exploit strong opponents
• Regularly check whether your exploitation still works

Use GTO as the default baseline and deviate only on opponent leaks that are backed by enough hands and point in one clear direction; size the deviation by "observable deviation × (1 - opponent adjustment probability)" — derivation in the formula below.

The GTO-exploitation unified framework:
Strategy = GTO baseline + directional deviation × magnitude cap

Directional deviation rules:
1. Opponent folds too much → increase bluff frequency
2. Opponent calls too much → tighten value range, reduce bluffs
3. Opponent raises too much → narrow your continuing range
4. Opponent raises too little → bet with a wider range

Magnitude cap formula:
Safe deviation = observable deviation × (1 - opponent adjustment probability)

Example: opponent flop C-Bet frequency 80% (equilibrium 60%, deviation +20%)
Assume opponent adjustment probability = 50% (mid-stakes players gradually notice your deviation)
Safe deviation = 20% × (1-0.5) = 10%
Your response: increase fold-to-C-Bet rate about 10%
Within the safe range, even if the opponent adjusts, you won't get counter-exploited

(Note: the higher the opponent's adjustment probability, the smaller the allowed deviation; as it approaches 1, pull the deviation back and return to the GTO baseline)

Theory reference: the full theory of the GTO-exploitation unified framework is in Theory Academy T9 Chapter 4 "The GTO-Exploitation Unified Framework", including the execution methodology of "using GTO as a baseline and making disciplined directional deviations based on observable deviations".

Counter-intuitive: GTO baseline + exploitative deviation = the optimal mixed strategy. This isn't choosing between GTO and exploitation — it's "starting from GTO and making minimal necessary deviations when spotting weaknesses". Deviation magnitude isn't "bigger is better"; operate within the range where "you still don't lose after the opponent adjusts".

Pool is too tight — increase bluffs

d-l8-pool-q5.question: The NL5 pool river-bets only 8%. How should you adjust?
d-l8-pool-q5.explanation: River bets at only 8% mean the pool is extremely passive — river bets are almost pure value. Call tight against river bets and fold medium hands.

option: Bet every time the opponent checks (including bluffs)
d-l8-pool-q6.explanation: Check-raising only 2% means the pool almost never raises. Bet every time the opponent checks to capture free value — no worry about being check-raised.

option: Defend with a wider range (better odds)
d-l8-pool-q7.explanation: A 2.2BB open means you get a better price in the BB (better pot odds). Defend wider (call/3-bet) because it's mathematically more favorable.

d-l8-pool-q8.scenario: You discover a stake's players fold to steals (SB/BTN open) only 40%
d-l8-pool-q8.question: The pool folds to steals only 40%. How should you adjust?
option: Reduce steal frequency, because opponents don't fold
d-l8-pool-q8.explanation: Folding to steals only 40% means the pool defends the blinds actively. Reduce steal frequency and open stronger hands, because bluff success is low.

d-l8-pool-q9.question: The pool folds 55% to turn C-Bets. How should you adjust?
option: Increase turn C-Bet frequency with a value + bluff mix
d-l8-pool-q9.explanation: 55% fold-to-turn-C-Bet means the pool is too weak on the turn. Increase C-Bet frequency (value + bluff mix) to capture lots of fold equity.
